extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, historians, and policymakers interested in colonial trade and governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and policy standards concerning colonial administration and trade (late 18th-century perspective). Emphasis on what kinds of regulations help or harm colonial improvement, commerce, and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality of civil establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil establishments of English colonies were inexpensive (examples: Pennsylvania £4500; New Jersey £1200; Virginia and South Carolina £8000), demonstrating how a large population can be well governed at small expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides example sums and contrasts with more expensive colonial administrations elsewhere; emphasizes that modest civil costs are compatible with good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mother country bears defence costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important part of government expense, defence and protection, has constantly fallen upon the mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that colonies benefit from defence borne by the metropole, reducing the colony's fiscal burden for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-cost ceremonial government
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial upon reception of a new governor or opening of an assembly is sufficiently decent but not accompanied with expensive pomp or parade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding costly ceremonial prevents introduction of vanity and expense into colonial society; reduces occasional grievous taxes and long-term tendencies to luxury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugal ecclesiastical government in English colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Tithes are unknown; clergy are few and maintained by moderate stipends or voluntary contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links light ecclesiastical burdens to less oppressive taxation and social costs, contrasting with Catholic colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial revenue extraction by Spain and Portugal
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of Spain and Portugal derives some support from the taxes levied upon their colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions Iberian policy as extracting revenue directly from colonies, unlike English practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expensive ceremonials encourage private luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive ceremonial expenditures (e.g., reception of a viceroy of Peru) are real taxes on colonists that introduce habits of vanity and perpetual private luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ceremonials create occasional grievous taxes and help establish ruinous taxes of private extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppressive ecclesiastical systems (tithes and mendicant friars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish and Portuguese colonies impose tithes and maintain a numerous race of mendicant friars whose beggary is consecrated by religion, burdening the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the social and economic harms of enforced religious exactions and clergy as large landholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive company monopolies stunt colony growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving the whole commerce of a colony to an exclusive company forces colonists to buy dear and sell cheap; companies buy only as much produce as they can resell at high European prices, discouraging colonial growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the company model as 'the most effectual' expedient to stunt natural growth of a new colony; cites Holland, Denmark, France, and Portugal examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confining colonial trade to a particular port fosters cartel-like abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring colonial trade to go through a single mother-country port, via fleets or licensed ships, enables merchants who combine stocks to act like an exclusive company and extract exorbitant profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how coordination among merchants leads to oppressive prices and poor supplies for colonies (example: Spanish West Indies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free intra-national competition benefits colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving trade free to all subjects trading from multiple ports prevents combination and excessive profits, enabling colonies to sell produce and buy European goods at reasonable prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites England (since dissolution of Plymouth company) and France as examples where more liberal policy produced less exorbitant prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated vs non-enumerated commodities principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain colonial products are 'enumerated' (must be exported to mother country) while 'non-enumerated' may be exported elsewhere in British/plantation ships with British owners and mariners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists examples of each and explains legal restrictions that shape colonial markets and metropolitan carrying trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage broad market for colonial grain
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing colonies a very extensive market for grain encourages them to cultivate beyond local consumption, providing subsistence for an increasing population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that market access is a direct incentive for agricultural expansion and long-term improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise timber value by opening market for lumber
rubrics_metrics.description: By allowing colonies an extensive market for lumber, the law raises the price of timber, facilitating clearing land and converting an expense into a profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that in heavily wooded colonies timber is initially of little value; market access makes improvement feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase cattle value via wider markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing American cattle a very extensive market raises their value, which is essential for land improvement because cattle price must bear a certain proportion to that of corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that enumerating hides and skins reduces the value of cattle (example: 4th Geo. III c. 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage fisheries to build shipping/naval power
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending and encouraging colonial fisheries increases shipping and naval power; New England and the whale fishery are cited as important examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions fisheries as strategic economic activity supporting carrying trade and maritime strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on colonial refining/manufacture discourage local industry
rubrics_metrics.description: High duties and prohibitions (e.g., on claying/refining sugar, steel furnaces, slit-mills) prevent colonies from establishing more advanced manufactures, reserving them for metropolitan merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides sugar-refining example: duties made colonial refining unprofitable in British colonies unlike French; also mentions prohibitions on steel works and internal trade restrictions that prevent woollen manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular-trade commodities (rum and slaves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rum is an important article in American trade to the African coast in exchange for negro slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies specific commodity roles within intercontinental trade patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid enumerating staples that would harm metropolitan industry balance
rubrics_metrics.description: If all colonial surplus (grain, salt provisions, fish) had been enumerated and forced into Great Britain's market, it would have interfered with domestic industry; thus imports of most grain and salt provisions have been prohibited into Great Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale for selectively keeping important staples off the enumeration to protect metropolitan producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic restrictions on non-enumerated exports
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-enumerated commodities allowed export to all parts of the world were later restricted (e.g., to parts of Europe south of Cape Finisterre by 6 Geo. III c. 52).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that such restrictions reflected concern about competing with domestic manufacturing regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold rationale for enumerated commodities
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated commodities include (1) peculiar colonial produce not producible at home, and (2) commodities producible at home but only in insufficient quantities; the first were confined to home market to establish a carrying trade, the second to protect domestic producers via duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains intended economic effects: cheaper colonial supply to home merchants and strategic discouragement of foreign producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unintended effects of combined regulations (bounties vs prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneous regulations (e.g., prohibiting foreign naval stores but giving bounties for American naval stores) can jointly encourage colonial production more than intended; combined effects may be accidental but real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Sweden pitch/tar episode and British bounty example showing policy interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated iron with duty exemptions can encourage local manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Though pig and bar iron are enumerated, exemption from duties when imported from America contributes to encouraging furnaces and iron manufacture in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that the form of regulation (enumeration plus duty exemptions) can have pro-development effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of trade between colonies fosters large internal markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect freedom of trade is permitted between British colonies of America and the West Indies, creating an internal market where colonies buy from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues this internal trade makes a substantial mutual market and supports colonial prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan reserve of refined manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Britain reserves more advanced or refined manufactures to its merchants and prevents their establishment in the colonies by duties or absolute prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames this as merchants/manufacturers protecting their interests; notes that because British manufactures can be imported cheaply, the prohibition is often an 'impertinent badge of slavery' rather than immediately harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal carriage/export prohibitions hinder provincial manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions on exportation between provinces by water or carriage by land of hats, wools, and woollen goods prevent the establishment of manufactures intended for distant sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules confine colonial industry to household-level manufactures and block larger-scale manufacture for export.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonists' right to manage affairs (representative assemblies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in foreign trade, the liberty of English colonists to manage their own affairs is complete: assemblies of representatives claim sole right to impose taxes and overawe executive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes institutional protections: assemblies appoint revenue officers, in places elect governors, and provide greater equality and republican manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-hereditary councils and colonial equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Councils in colonial legislatures do not consist of hereditary nobility; descendants of old families have respect but no hereditary privileges; generally more equality than at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects these institutional features to the more republican character of some colonies (e.g., New England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute metropolitan governments produce harsher colonial rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute governments of Spain, Portugal, and France take place in their colonies, and discretionary powers exercised at distance are naturally more violent and oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that remoteness amplifies tyranny because the sovereign's restraining presence is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary governments can provide protection to slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: In arbitrary governments the magistrate's willingness to interpose can protect slaves against masters' violence more easily than in free governments where magistrates hesitate to interfere in private property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Roman example (Vidius Pollio and Augustus) to argue that slaves' condition may paradoxically be better under certain arbitrary regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of slaves affects productivity and loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The good management of slaves (gentle usage, protection) makes them more faithful, intelligent, and useful—approaching condition of free servants—and thus more profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares French and English planters; claims French planters generally managed slaves better, an advantage in sugar colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of colonial capital matter for long-term improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement of French sugar colonies (e.g., St Domingo) was mainly funded by the gradual accumulation of colonial produce and industry, while English sugar colonies received much capital sent from England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies internal accumulation fosters durable improvement, whereas external capital inflows have different effects on colonial development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan merchant influence skews regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants carrying on colonial trade were principal advisers of many regulations; thus merchant interests often took precedence over those of the colonies or the mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how merchants sought to minimize costs and maximize drawbacks/rebates, and how that could harm national revenue and manufactures (example: German linen drawbacks retarding British linen manufacture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawbacks on duties to facilitate carrying trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Britain allowed part or all of import duties to be drawn back upon re-exportation to colonies, to keep the carrying trade viable; this was curtailed by 1763 legislation which reduced those drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the economic logic: without drawbacks foreign goods would be too costly in colonies and carrying trade would collapse; cites 4 Geo. III c. 15 limitation in 1763.
